title: Same Average, Different Risk
objective: After this level you can explain why two choices with the same expected value can differ in how badly things might go.
summary: Two bets can share an expected value and still be very different: a sure $50 and a coin flip for $100 or nothing both average $50. Expected value hides the spread, so also ask how bad it can get.

cards.headline: A: $50 for sure. B: flip a coin for $100 or nothing. Which do you take?
cards.body: Level 32's number calls them equal: both have an expected value of $50. Most people still grab the sure thing. They aren't bad at math.

cards.headline: The average hides the spread
cards.body: Both choices average $50, but look at what can actually happen. A pays exactly $50 every time. B pays $100 or $0, and never $50. Expected value squeezes all the outcomes into one average, so it can't show how far apart they are. Two bets can share an average and still be very different bets.

mascot.line: Keep this: expected value gives you the middle, not the edges. Always ask how bad it can get.

cards.headline: Same average, bigger stakes
cards.body: Now two coin bets. In one, you win or lose $1. In the other, you win or lose $1,000. Both have an expected value of $0, since the win and the loss cancel out. But only the second can cost you $1,000 on one bad flip. When the worst case is something you couldn't afford, the spread matters more than the average.

cards.fact: Risk-averse people prefer a sure thing to a gamble with the same expected value.
cards.context: That's a preference about risk, not an arithmetic error. It's why insurance sells (Level 35), and why a fair-looking bet can still be a poor idea. So judge any gamble on two things: its average, and how bad it can get.

cards.headline: Risk: measured
learned: A sure $50 and a $100-or-nothing flip both average $50
Same average, bigger stakes, bigger worst case
Judge a bet by its average and how bad it can get

questions.prompt: A sure $50 and a coin flip for $100 or nothing have _____ in common.

options.label: the same worst case
options.rationale: The sure $50 can't pay $0; the flip can.

questions.explanation: Half of $100 plus half of $0 is $50, the same as the sure thing.

questions.prompt: How can two bets with the same expected value differ in risk?

options.label: Their outcomes can be close together or far apart
One must have a higher average after all
options.rationale: Both averages can be exactly the same.

options.label: Expected value changes each time you play
options.rationale: It stays the same; the actual results vary.

options.label: Only bets with positive expected value are risky
options.rationale: A $0 expected value bet can still cost $1,000.

questions.explanation: Expected value squeezes outcomes into one average, so it hides how far apart they are, like $1 against $1,000 stakes.

questions.prompt: Insurance swaps a big possible loss for a small, sure cost. In this level's terms, what does it do?

options.label: Raises your expected value
options.rationale: Buyers lose a little on average, so it lowers it slightly.

options.label: Removes every possible loss
options.rationale: You still pay the premium every year.

options.label: Narrows the spread of outcomes, at a small cost to the average
Leaves both the spread and the average unchanged
options.rationale: It cuts the worst case sharply.

questions.explanation: Premiums cost a little more than the expected loss, but the huge worst case is gone.
